# Workforce Participation Trajectories

Tracked from graduation through 10+ years out, the data shows a population that sorts itself into a stable, familiar shape fairly quickly and then holds it. Regional employment (Northeast Minnesota specifically) grows for years before leveling off — meaningful regional employment climbs from the immediate post-graduation period and peaks around **year 6, at nearly 30% of graduates working 1,000+ hours for a single regional employer**. Employment anywhere in Minnesota is broader still: **by year 6, nearly half of all graduates have meaningful employment somewhere in the state.** But disconnection doesn't resolve the way instability does — **graduates falling short of the meaningful-employment threshold hovers around 20% from as early as one year out**, and critically, **the "no Minnesota employment record" group keeps growing rather than shrinking, reaching nearly 30% of all graduates by year 10.** This is the trajectory that motivated the deeper dive into persistence: early instability mostly resolves into something else (regional work, statewide work, or postsecondary study), but disappearing from Minnesota's tracked labor market behaves differently — it's the one outcome that keeps climbing the longer you look.

<br>

## Pathway 1: College Completers

This is the pathway most clearly built around **whether, where, and what level of credential** a graduate completes — three separate, independently important levers, not one.

**Completing any postsecondary credential is a large, independent driver of regional workforce attachment on its own.** Among the full graduating population, having completed a credential raises the odds of sustained regional employment substantially (**`ps.grad`: OR ≈ 1.72**) — holding up fully alongside every demographic, geographic, and academic-engagement variable in the model.

**But *where* that credential was earned matters more than almost anything else measured in this entire project.** Among completers, graduating from a postsecondary institution within the region is the single largest predictor of sustained regional employment found anywhere across all these analyses (**`ps.grad.location`: OR ≈ 3.22**) — more than triple the odds relative to completing elsewhere in Minnesota. This one variable substantially explains away several other effects that looked independent before it entered the model, including much of the apparent advantage of sub-baccalaureate credentials and some district-geography effects.

**Credential level also matters independently, on top of location.** Completers whose highest credential is an Associate degree or less show meaningfully higher odds of regional attachment than Bachelor's-degree holders (**`highest.cred.level`, Associate-or-lesser: OR ≈ 1.40–1.78** depending on whether location is controlled) — sub-baccalaureate, technical-oriented credentials are simply more tied to the regional economy by design.

**Academic engagement in high school splits into two opposing signals for this pathway, and the direction flips depending on which side of the ledger you're looking at.** Simply taking the ACT predicts *completing* a credential at a much lower rate (**`took.ACT`: OR ≈ 0.56** for overall completion) but, among those who do complete, predicts *staying regional* at a dramatically higher rate (**OR ranging from ≈ 2.9 up to ≈ 6.6 to 14** depending on the specific completion outcome) — while a strong ACT score among test-takers consistently predicts the opposite: leaving for a four-year degree, often outside the region (**`ACTCompositeScore`: OR consistently below 1, ranging ≈ 0.82–0.96 per point** across every model in this pathway). AP exam participation and SAT-taking both reinforce the "leaving" side of this same story (**both consistently OR \< 1** for regional attachment and regional completion). PSEO participation, meanwhile, plays a genuinely different role depending on the specific outcome — a strong, mechanical predictor of *completion itself* (**OR ≈ 1.65**, since it directly provides college credit) but not an independent predictor of *where* someone ends up afterward.

**Demographic disparities in this pathway are real but not uniform.** Economic disadvantage and Special Education status both show very large, negative bivariate-adjacent relationships with completion (**OR ≈ 0.36 and 0.27 respectively** in the demographics-only model), and while academic engagement explains a meaningful share of both, **neither is fully explained away** (both remain significant, in the **OR ≈ 0.48** range, once accomplishments are considered). Black, Hispanic, and American Indian graduates all show independently lower odds of completing a credential at all (**Black OR ≈ 0.66, Hispanic OR ≈ 0.68, American Indian OR ≈ 0.69**, fully adjusted), and Asian/Pacific Islander graduates show a real, if more variable, disadvantage that only becomes visible once academic engagement is considered. **English learner status behaves in the single most important and clarifying way found in this pathway:** it's a strong, independent predictor of reduced regional attachment for the full population (**OR ≈ 0.74**, holding up through every model including full postsecondary completion) — but among students who actually complete a credential, it shows **no relationship at all** with regional attachment, completion location, or credential level. The English learner disparity in this data is a story about workforce attachment for those who don't complete college — it is not an academic-preparation story, and it fully resolves once a credential is in hand.

<br>

## Pathway 2: Workforce First — Sustained Regional Employment Without a Credential

Among non-college graduates who *do* achieve sustained regional employment, **one signal dominates everything else, and it strengthens rather than fades over time: Career and Technical Education engagement.**

**CTE achievement is the single most consistent, and the only strengthening, predictor identified anywhere in this analysis.** Across every time horizon examined — one year, five years, and ten years post-graduation — CTE Concentrator/Completer status raises the odds of sustained regional employment (**OR ≈ 1.38–1.53**, actually *growing* larger at the 10-year mark rather than fading), and CTE Participant status shows a smaller but equally consistent effect (**OR ≈ 1.14–1.25**). No other variable in this entire pathway behaves this way — everything else weakens, disappears, or shifts direction somewhere in the ten-year window; CTE just keeps getting stronger.

**ACT shows the same participation/score crossover found in the college-completer pathway, but somewhat more modestly.** Simply taking the ACT predicts higher odds of sustained regional employment at every time point (**OR ≈ 1.97–2.94**, largest at Year 1, weakening by Year 10), while a higher composite score among test-takers predicts the opposite (**OR ≈ 0.94–0.96 per point**) — the same "engagement helps, strong performance pulls away" pattern, just less pronounced than among college-bound peers.

**PSEO participation and district geography both play smaller, more time-limited roles than they do elsewhere in this project.** PSEO shows a real, positive, independent relationship with sustained regional employment only in the first year after graduation (**OR ≈ 1.13**) and no relationship at all by Year 5 or Year 10 — its benefit for this specific pathway looks front-loaded rather than lasting. District classification shows no relationship at Year 1, emerges as significant by Year 5 (Urban/town-rural mix districts, **OR ≈ 1.44**), then fades to only marginal significance by Year 10 — geography's role here appears to build gradually rather than mattering from the start, and unlike almost every other pathway examined in this project, **Range school status, local wages, and local unemployment rate show essentially no relationship with this outcome at any point** — geography and the local economy simply matter less here than what happened in high school.

**Demographic disparities in this pathway are durable, and in the two clearest cases, they widen rather than close over a decade.** Black graduates show the single largest and most consistent disparity found in this pathway, growing from **OR ≈ 0.52 at Year 1 to OR ≈ 0.30 by Year 10** — roughly a two-thirds reduction in odds by the ten-year mark. Gender shows the same widening pattern (**OR ≈ 0.94 at Year 1 down to OR ≈ 0.77 at Year 10**), with women showing steadily lower odds of sustained regional employment the further out the window extends. English learner status, Special Education status, and Hispanic identity all show strong, independent, even strengthening disparities at Year 1 and Year 5 (**English learner OR ≈ 0.63–0.74; Special Ed OR ≈ 0.67–0.85**) that become statistically undetectable by Year 10 — but given how consistently these held up in the two earlier, better-powered models, this is much more likely a sample-size limitation at the ten-year mark than evidence the disparities have actually resolved.

<br>

## Pathway 3: Disconnected — Persistent Non-Sustained Employment and No Minnesota Employment Record

This pathway is where the redone analysis makes its sharpest refinement to the original framework: **"disconnection" splits cleanly into two different, largely independent mechanisms, and different groups experience each one.**

**Special Education status is an instability story, not a no-record story — one of the most reliable findings in this entire project.** Special Ed status is a strong, significant, *independent* predictor of persistent unstable employment (**OR ≈ 1.36–1.45**, holding steady across every level of control) but shows **no relationship whatsoever with persistent no-record status** at any stage. This is a genuine reversal from what the bivariate pattern initially suggested, and it holds up robustly.

**English learner status, and the Hispanic, Black, and Asian/Pacific Islander disparities, are a no-record story, not (primarily) an instability story — and these are among the most robust findings in this entire project.** English learner status shows one of the strongest, most independent relationships with persistent no-record status found anywhere (**OR ≈ 1.71–1.94**, barely attenuating across every level of control), while showing no significant relationship with instability specifically. Hispanic (**OR ≈ 2.29–2.42**) and Asian/Pacific Islander graduates (**OR ≈ 2.12–2.41**) both show similarly large, fully independent elevations in persistent no-record status — Asian/Pacific Islander graduates show a striking divergence, with *reduced* odds of instability alongside among the *highest* odds of no-record status of any group. Black graduates show real, independent elevated risk on **both** fronts (**no-record OR ≈ 1.41–1.47; instability OR ≈ 1.68–1.74**), while American Indian graduates' disadvantage sits almost entirely on the instability side (**OR ≈ 1.37–1.39**) with no corresponding no-record effect.

**Economic status and Gender each show a genuine split-personality pattern across the two mechanisms.** Economically disadvantaged graduates show *no* elevated instability risk but a real, independent *protective* relationship with no-record status (**OR ≈ 0.72–0.78**). Female graduates show the same divided pattern in reverse: modestly elevated instability risk (**OR ≈ 1.31–1.34**) alongside a real, independent protective relationship with no-record status (**OR ≈ 0.87–0.89**).

**Academic engagement and postsecondary attempt both show strong, mechanism-specific effects that mirror the other two pathways.** Attempting postsecondary education — even without completing it — is protective against both forms of disconnection independently (**instability OR ≈ 0.72; no-record OR ≈ 0.53**), confirming this is the one variable that meaningfully touches both mechanisms. CTE achievement and PSEO participation are both strongly, independently protective against no-record status specifically (**CTE OR ≈ 0.69–0.75; PSEO OR ≈ 0.75–0.76**) but show little independent relationship with instability. Taking the ACT is the single strongest predictor of avoiding no-record status found in this entire pathway (**OR ≈ 0.26–0.30** — roughly a 70–74% reduction in odds), while showing a much smaller, adverse relationship with instability specifically (**OR ≈ 1.21–1.22**, students who take the ACT but don't complete college show a mild *increase* in instability risk).

<br>

### Putting It Together

The three-pathway framework holds up well under the redone methodology, and the corrections made along the way — dropping MCA Math as an unreliable control, adding Range school status and SAT participation, and testing English learner status everywhere it had previously been assumed away — mostly sharpened the story rather than overturning it. The clearest throughline across all three pathways is this: **credentials, CTE engagement, and postsecondary location/attempt are the levers most within reach of workforce and education systems, and they behave consistently and predictably across every pathway examined.** Demographic disparities, by contrast, are real, often large, and — critically — **attach to specific mechanisms rather than to disconnection broadly**: Special Ed and American Indian disadvantage is an instability story; English learner, Hispanic, and Asian/Pacific Islander disadvantage is a no-record story; and Black graduates alone show a substantial, independent disadvantage on every front measured, in every pathway, at every time horizon.
